children: By Erin Mulvaney, Cara Lombardo and Alexander Gladstone
Weil, Gotshal & Manges leaders are searching for a path to stabilize the law firm, whose future is growing more uncertain by the day.

The firm's management committee met uninterrupted for all of Sunday to discuss the firm's future, and renewed talks on Monday, people familiar with the matter said. The committee's ranks have already been reduced as several of its members are leaving for rivals.

A member of Weil's leadership team recently reached out to restructuring counsel at another firm seeking guidance on options should the situation continue to deteriorate, other people familiar with the matter said. Davis Polk represented Weil Gotshal in merger talks that fell through last week and is continuing to advise the firm, said another person familiar with the matter who declined to comment specifically on what.

Internal anxiety about the firm's survival intensified after the merger talks failed. News also broke that at least four additional top partners are departing for rival firms and the firm's would-be incoming leader no longer plans to take the role.

Partners in several different practice groups around the firm are frantically sending résumés to rival firms, including Sidley Austin, White & Case, and Simpson Thacher, according to people familiar with the matter.

Questions also mounted about the future of two of the top revenue-generating firm leaders, who are being heavily courted by rivals. If both depart and bring with them members of their practice groups, it could deal a potentially decisive blow to the firm, people in the industry say.

Matt Barr, the global chair of Weil's restructuring practice, has been getting calls from other firms about potentially leaving and bringing several of his top lawyers with him, people familiar with the matter said. Barr in recent weeks told his partners that he didn't have plans to leave, other people say.

Private-equity partner Ramona Nee, who was elected as the firm's leader earlier this year to succeed Barry Wolf, told the firm in September she wouldn't take the role, according to people familiar with the matter. Nee doesn't have immediate plans to leave but many firms have expressed interest in recruiting her and her team, some of the people said.
The Financial Times earlier reported Nee's decision to step down but not the timing.

Last month, The Wall Street Journal reported that Michael Aiello, who led Weil's more than 600-person corporate practice, is set to join Cravath along with other M&A-focused partners, a major blow to the firm's future.

Founded in 1931, Weil was a pioneer among elite firms in building a restructuring practice, leading some of the largest bankruptcies in history, including those of Lehman Brothers, General Motors and Enron. Now a firm that made its name shepherding companies through bankruptcy is facing mounting financial pressure itself if it can't stem partner losses or find a merger partner.
It is an extraordinary turn of events for a firm that last year brought in $2.1 billion in revenue and over $5.6 million in profits per equity partner, according to American Lawyer data.

Among its liabilities: A lease for some 380,000 square feet at the General Motors Building across from Central Park in Manhattan, according to CoStar Group. One of the people familiar with the matter said that Weil has been examining its lease obligations in recent days.
